summary: Introduces terminology to categorize types of YANG modules. YANG is used by many organizations, but there was no well-known vocabulary for the kinds of modules. Consistent terms help analysis and discussion between groups.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8199 gives names for two aspects of a YANG module: the level of network it describes and who produced it. These categories help people discuss modules consistently.

questions: how do you categorize yang modules
subtitle: A two-dimensional vocabulary for classifying YANG modules

tldr.problem: Many groups publish YANG modules, but there was no common terminology for describing their abstraction level and origin.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8199 proposes two classification dimensions: Network Service or Network Element abstraction, and Standard, Vendor-Specific, or User-Specific origin.
tldr.outcome: The taxonomy is intended to support clearer discussion and analysis of YANG modules. The RFC notes that category boundaries can be unclear and may change with experience.

today: RFC 8199 is an Informational document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes terminology for classifying YANG modules.

sections.title: Why Classify YANG Modules
sections.content:
Standards development organizations, open-source projects, vendors, and users publish YANG modules for many networking applications. RFC 8199 observes that there was no widely known terminology for categorizing them.

The document proposes a taxonomy to help people analyze YANG modeling work and communicate about modules. It states that classification boundaries can be unclear and that the criteria may change as the community gains experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Different groups create YANG modules, but they did not share names for the kinds of modules they created. This RFC proposes a common vocabulary.

sections.title: The Abstraction Layer
sections.content:
A Network Element YANG Module describes configuration, state, operations, or notifications for a specific device technology or feature. Examples include interfaces, routing protocols, and access control lists.

A Network Service YANG Module describes an abstract service implemented across one or more network elements. An orchestrator can decompose the service data into device-level configuration. The document says the service-to-element decomposition is separate from the module itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A Network Element module describes a device or feature. A Network Service module describes a service across devices, which an orchestrator can translate into device settings.

sections.title: The Module Origin
sections.content:
Standard YANG Modules are published by standards development organizations, such as the IETF or IEEE. Their lifecycle follows the standards process rather than a particular product release.

Vendor-Specific modules support implementations produced by vendors, consortia, or open-source projects, and their lifecycle often follows product or project releases. User-Specific modules are created by organizations operating YANG-based infrastructure to express needs beyond what vendor modules provide. Extensions may augment earlier modules, and real deployments can combine all three origin types.
sections.plainLanguage: Modules may come from standards groups, vendors or projects, or the organization operating the network. A deployment may use modules from all three sources.

sections.title: Using Both Dimensions
sections.content:
The abstraction and origin dimensions are independent. A module may be classified by what it describes and by who produced it. For example, the RFC notes that an L2VPN module could describe a service or could define L2VPN data for one device; the module name alone does not settle the classification.

The taxonomy can help operators identify modules for service composition, help vendors explain relationships among supported modules, and support discussions between standards organizations. The RFC presents the categories as a starting point, not rigid rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Classify a module both by its abstraction level and by its origin. Its name alone may not tell you which abstraction it represents.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 8199 states that it has no Security Considerations. It also states that no IANA actions are required.

The document's purpose is to describe concepts and terms for classifying modules; it does not specify a YANG protocol or data model.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not define a protocol or require changes to an IANA registry. It offers terminology for discussing YANG modules.
